Historical observations for this pairing come from several hundred weather stations across the contiguous United States that have collected data consistently for many decades. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) stores their records and makes them publicly available.

Model outputs are based on a set of 16 global climate models that reflect scientists’ current understanding of how greenhouse gases warm the atmosphere and how this heat moves between the atmosphere, water, and land. These same 16 models were used in the most recent National Climate Assessment. The modeled lines are smoother than the historical trends because the project team averaged 16 models together and also applied an 11-year smoothing filter, both of which smooth out year-to-year variability. However, the shaded bands do include year-to-year variability.

This feature defines “frost” days based on daily air temperature measurements or model outputs below the freezing point of 32°F. The graph shows annual anomalies, or the difference in growing season length relative to the average growing season length from 1895 to 2023.

Scientists usually use climate models to study how temperatures are expected to change over time, rather than to predict exact temperatures. This is because, although models generally agree on overall trends, factors like local climate differences and model biases can cause variation in the exact temperature values they produce.[1] Because the growing season indicator depends on counting the number of days above a specific temperature (32°F), it may have more uncertainty due to these variations in absolute temperature predictions across climate models.
